events.title: Moravian mission to enslaved Africans on St Thomas
events.summary: Leonhard Dober and David Nitschmann sailed from Herrnhut to the Danish West Indies to preach to enslaved Africans — the first Protestant mission to the enslaved. Under Friedrich Martin, Afro-Caribbean congregations formed with Black helpers such as Rebecca Protten.
causes: Herrnhut revival and Zinzendorf's missionary vision

events.title: First Great Awakening
events.summary: Revival began under Jonathan Edwards in Northampton (1734–35) and swept the American colonies with George Whitefield's open-air preaching tours (1739–41), paralleling awakenings in Wales, Scotland and England. Converts testified to the 'new birth'; critics deplored emotional excess, splitting churches into New and Old Lights.

events.title: John Wesley's Aldersgate experience
events.summary: On 24 May 1738, hearing Luther's preface to Romans read at a Moravian society meeting, John Wesley felt his 'heart strangely warmed' and received assurance that Christ had taken away his sins. Within a year he took to field preaching and organised the Methodist societies.
causes: Wesley's spiritual struggles and Moravian influence

events.title: The Philokalia published
events.summary: Nikodemos the Hagiorite and Makarios of Corinth compiled the Philokalia, an anthology of hesychast texts from the 4th to 15th centuries, printed in Venice. Paisius Velichkovsky's Slavonic version (1793) fuelled a Russian revival of eldership (startsy) and the Jesus Prayer.

events.title: Self-founded Catholic church in Korea
events.summary: Korean scholars studying Catholic books from China sent Yi Seung-hun to Beijing, where he was baptised in 1784; on returning he baptised others, founding a church without missionaries. Repeated persecutions (1791, 1801, 1839, 1866) produced thousands of martyrs, including Andrew Kim Taegon (1846).
causes: Silhak scholars' interest in Western learning

events.title: First Christian service in Australia
events.summary: The Anglican chaplain Richard Johnson held the first Christian service in Australia on 3 February 1788 for the convicts and marines of the First Fleet. Christianity in Australia began as a chaplaincy to a penal colony, while Aboriginal peoples experienced dispossession.
consequences: Anglican, Catholic and Protestant churches of Australia

events.title: Baptist Missionary Society founded
events.summary: Inspired by William Carey's Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens, Particular Baptist ministers founded a missionary society at Kettering. Carey sailed for India in 1793; the BMS inaugurated the age of voluntary Protestant mission societies.
causes: Carey's argument from the Great Commission
consequences: LMS (1795), CMS (1799) and many more societies

events.title: Black Christian settlers found Freetown
events.summary: About 1,100 Black Loyalists from Nova Scotia — many Baptist, Methodist and Countess of Huntingdon's Connexion Christians — sailed to Sierra Leone and founded Freetown, arriving singing hymns. Freetown became the base for West African Christianity, later home to recaptives like Samuel Ajayi Crowther.
causes: American Revolution and British promises of freedom
consequences: First Protestant churches in West Africa led by Africans

events.title: LMS missionaries land on Tahiti
events.summary: The ship Duff landed thirty London Missionary Society artisans and ministers at Matavai Bay. After years of hardship, chief Pōmare II converted (1812), and Tahitian and other Islander evangelists carried Christianity across Polynesia, often faster than European missionaries.
consequences: Islander missionaries to Samoa, Fiji and beyond

events.title: Second Great Awakening
events.summary: A prolonged wave of revivals in the early United States, from frontier camp meetings to Charles Finney's urban campaigns, made Methodists and Baptists the largest denominations and spawned reform movements — temperance, abolition, missions — and new religious bodies.
consequences: Restorationist and new movements, including Adventism and Latter-day Saints

events.title: Serampore mission and Bible translation
events.summary: William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward settled in Danish Serampore, establishing a press that printed Scripture in some 40 Indian and Asian languages, a college (1818) and schools. Carey's opposition to sati contributed to its abolition (1829).
causes: East India Company hostility to missionaries in British territory

events.title: Cane Ridge camp meeting
events.summary: In August 1801 perhaps 10,000–20,000 people gathered at Cane Ridge for a week-long Presbyterian communion that became a revival with Methodist and Baptist preachers; many fell, jerked or shouted. Barton Stone, its host, later helped found the Restoration Movement.

events.title: Britain abolishes the slave trade
events.summary: After a twenty-year campaign led in Parliament by the evangelical William Wilberforce, with Quakers, the Clapham Sect and formerly enslaved writers like Olaudah Equiano, Britain outlawed the Atlantic slave trade. Slavery itself was abolished in the British Empire in 1833.

events.title: Robert Morrison begins Protestant mission in China
events.summary: Robert Morrison of the London Missionary Society arrived in Canton, working for the East India Company as translator. He completed a Chinese Bible (1823) with William Milne and a Chinese–English dictionary, but baptised only a handful of converts.

events.title: Samuel Marsden preaches in New Zealand
events.summary: On Christmas Day 1814, Samuel Marsden preached on Luke 2:10 at Oihi with the support of the Ngāpuhi chief Ruatara, who translated. Māori conversion grew rapidly from the 1830s, often led by Māori evangelists, and Christianity shaped the Treaty of Waitangi (1840).

events.title: African Methodist Episcopal Church founded
events.summary: After being pulled from their knees in St George's Methodist Church, Richard Allen and Black Methodists founded Bethel Church and, in 1816, the African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first independent Black denomination in the United States.
consequences: AME missions in Africa and the Caribbean

events.title: American missionaries arrive in Hawai'i
events.summary: Missionaries of the American Board arrived months after the abolition of the kapu system; Queen Kaʻahumanu became a Christian and promoted the faith. Missionaries created a written Hawaiian language, schools and churches, and some descendants later joined the economic elite that overthrew the monarchy (1893).

events.title: Persecution of Christians in Madagascar
events.summary: Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity, expelled LMS missionaries and executed many Malagasy believers, some thrown from the cliffs of Ampamarinana. The underground church grew; after her death the court converted (1869) and Protestantism became dominant in the highlands.

events.title: Niger Expedition and Crowther's ordination
events.summary: A British expedition up the Niger to promote 'Christianity and commerce' and end the slave trade lost many Europeans to fever, but the Yoruba recaptive Samuel Ajayi Crowther's journal impressed the CMS, which had him ordained in London in 1843. Henry Venn's vision of self-governing African churches followed.
causes: Abolitionist strategy of Thomas Fowell Buxton

events.title: The Great Disappointment
events.summary: Followers of the Baptist preacher William Miller expected Christ's return on 22 October 1844 based on calculations from Daniel 8:14. When it did not happen, the movement fragmented; one group reinterpreted the date as Christ entering the heavenly sanctuary and, with Ellen G. White, formed the Seventh-day Adventist Church (1863).
consequences: Later influence on the Bible Student movement

events.title: Taiping Rebellion
events.summary: Hong Xiuquan, after reading a Protestant tract and visionary experiences, proclaimed himself Jesus' younger brother and led the 'Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace' from Nanjing. The civil war cost perhaps 20 million lives and left lasting Chinese suspicion of Christianity as subversive.

events.title: Dogma of the Immaculate Conception
events.summary: In the bull Ineffabilis Deus (8 December 1854), Pius IX defined that Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception by a singular grace in view of Christ's merits. It was the first dogma proclaimed by a pope on his own authority after consulting bishops.
causes: Long-standing devotion and Franciscan theology (Duns Scotus)

events.title: Crowther's Niger Mission at Onitsha
events.summary: Samuel Ajayi Crowther founded the CMS Niger Mission with an all-African staff at Onitsha. Consecrated bishop in Canterbury Cathedral in 1864, he became the first African Anglican bishop; European missionaries later undermined him, and his forced resignation (1890) prompted African church independence movements.
consequences: African independent churches after Crowther's humiliation

events.title: China Inland Mission founded
events.summary: Hudson Taylor founded the China Inland Mission, interdenominational and faith-based, whose missionaries wore Chinese dress and went into all the interior provinces. The Lammermuir party reached Hangzhou in 1866. By 1900 it was the largest Protestant mission in China.

events.title: First Vatican Council
events.summary: Pius IX's council defined in Pastor aeternus (18 July 1870) the pope's universal jurisdiction and his infallibility when speaking ex cathedra on faith and morals. A minority left Rome rather than vote no; the council was suspended when Italian troops took Rome. Dissenters in Germany, Switzerland and Austria formed the Old Catholic churches.
events.longText: Vatican I took place amid the loss of the Papal States and the Catholic Church's struggle with liberalism, rationalism and nation-states. The constitution Dei Filius affirmed that God can be known by natural reason and that faith and reason cannot conflict. Pastor aeternus taught that the Roman pontiff, when he defines doctrine ex cathedra, possesses the infallibility Christ willed his church to have, and that such definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not from the consent of the church'. Some 60 bishops of the minority, including leading German and French prelates, considered the definition inopportune or historically problematic (the case of Honorius) and left before the final vote. Ignaz von Döllinger refused to accept it and was excommunicated; the Old Catholic churches formed and joined the Union of Utrecht (1889). Orthodox and Protestants saw the definition as the decisive barrier to reunion. Catholic theology since Vatican II has set infallibility within the collegiality of bishops and the sense of the faithful, and only one later definition (1950) is universally regarded as ex cathedra.

events.title: Uganda martyrs
events.summary: Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda executed Catholic and Anglican pages and courtiers who refused his demands, burning 32 alive at Namugongo on 3 June 1886, among them Charles Lwanga. Their deaths fuelled rapid growth of both churches; the Catholic martyrs were canonised in 1964.
causes: Political struggle at the Buganda court
Christians' refusal of the king's sexual demands

events.title: Rerum Novarum and Catholic social teaching
events.summary: Leo XIII's encyclical on capital and labour defended private property against socialism while affirming workers' rights to a just wage and to form unions. It launched modern Catholic social teaching, developed by later popes.

events.title: Boxer Uprising
events.summary: The anti-foreign Boxer movement, with Qing support, killed some 32,000 Chinese Catholics, 2,000 Protestants and over 200 missionaries in northern China, notably at Taiyuan in Shanxi. Foreign armies crushed the uprising and imposed indemnities; Chinese Christians' sufferings were later honoured by both Catholics and Protestants.

events.title: Welsh Revival
events.summary: The young ex-miner Evan Roberts led meetings marked by spontaneous prayer, singing and confession, beginning at Loughor in November 1904. Some 100,000 conversions were reported in Wales within months, with reports inspiring revivals in India, Korea and Los Angeles.
consequences: Inspiration for Azusa Street and Pyongyang

events.title: Mukti revival in India
events.summary: At Pandita Ramabai's Mukti Mission for widows and orphaned girls, prayer for revival led in 1905 to intense repentance, visions and, by some reports, speaking in tongues. It is often cited as an Indian origin of Pentecostalism independent of North America.
causes: Ramabai's prayer bands inspired by Welsh reports

events.title: Azusa Street Revival
events.summary: William J. Seymour, an African American Holiness preacher taught by Charles Parham, led meetings at the Apostolic Faith Mission on Azusa Street from April 1906, where Black, white, Latino and Asian worshippers spoke in tongues and reported healings. Missionaries spread the message within two years to some 50 countries.
events.longText: Seymour had accepted Parham's teaching that speaking in tongues is the initial evidence of baptism in the Holy Spirit, though Parham's segregation forced him to listen from outside the classroom. Invited to Los Angeles, he was locked out of a Holiness church and began meetings in a home on Bonnie Brae Street, where tongues broke out on 9 April 1906; the meetings moved to a former AME building at 312 Azusa Street. Its newspaper, The Apostolic Faith, reached tens of thousands. Visitors noted the interracial character — 'the color line was washed away in the blood' — a striking contrast with Jim Crow America, though racial divisions soon re-emerged, including Parham's own denunciation. Critics mocked the noise and claimed demonic influence; Pentecostals see it as a latter-rain outpouring. Historians stress Azusa's catalytic role while noting parallel revivals in Wales, India (Mukti), Korea and Chile. The Pentecostal and charismatic movements descending from these currents now number hundreds of millions.

events.title: Pyongyang Great Revival
events.summary: During a Bible class at Jangdaehyun Church in January 1907, Korean elder Kil Seon-ju and others led public confession of sins that spread through the Presbyterian and Methodist churches. Early-morning prayer and Bible study became hallmarks of Korean Protestantism; Pyongyang was called the 'Jerusalem of the East'.

events.title: Scofield Reference Bible
events.summary: Cyrus I. Scofield's annotated King James Bible built Darby's dispensational premillennialism into its notes, dividing history into seven dispensations and distinguishing Israel and the church. It sold millions and shaped fundamentalist and evangelical eschatology for generations.

events.title: World Missionary Conference, Edinburgh
events.summary: Some 1,200 delegates of Protestant mission societies, chaired by John R. Mott, met to plan 'the evangelisation of the world in this generation'. Only about 18 delegates were from Asia; V. S. Azariah's plea 'give us friends' became famous. Its continuation committee led to the International Missionary Council and the ecumenical movement.

events.title: The Fundamentals published
events.summary: Funded by oil businessmen Lyman and Milton Stewart, ninety essays in twelve volumes defended biblical inerrancy, the virgin birth, substitutionary atonement, bodily resurrection and miracles against higher criticism and liberal theology. Distributed free to clergy, they gave the name 'fundamentalist' to the movement.

events.title: William Wade Harris's mass movement
events.summary: The Liberian Grebo prophet William Wade Harris, in white robe with cross, Bible and calabash, walked along the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast calling people to burn fetishes and be baptised. Perhaps 100,000–120,000 people converted in eighteen months before French authorities expelled him; Methodist and Harrist churches grew from his work.
causes: Harris's prison vision of the angel Gabriel

events.title: Armenian genocide and Sayfo
events.summary: During World War I the Ottoman government deported and massacred an estimated one million or more Armenians, along with Syriac (Assyrian) Christians in the Sayfo ('sword') and Greeks of Anatolia. Death marches ended in the Syrian desert at Deir ez-Zor. The ancient Christian presence in Anatolia was nearly erased.
causes: Ottoman wartime nationalism and fear of Christian minorities
consequences: Canonisation of the martyrs by the Armenian Church (2015)

events.title: Fátima apparitions
events.summary: Three shepherd children — Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta — reported six appearances of the Virgin Mary between May and October 1917, calling for prayer, penance and the consecration of Russia. On 13 October a crowd reported the 'miracle of the sun'. The church approved the devotion in 1930.
causes: Wartime anxieties and Portuguese anticlerical republic

events.title: Moscow Council restores the patriarchate; Bolshevik persecution begins
events.summary: The All-Russian Church Council restored the patriarchate and elected Tikhon in November 1917, days after the Bolshevik revolution. The Soviet state separated church and state, confiscated property and launched persecutions that killed tens of thousands of clergy and believers in the following decades.
consequences: Catacomb church and Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia

events.title: Simon Kimbangu's healing ministry
events.summary: Simon Kimbangu, a Baptist catechist in the Belgian Congo, began a healing and preaching ministry at Nkamba in April 1921 that drew crowds and emptied mission churches. Arrested within months and sentenced to death (commuted), he spent thirty years in prison; his followers formed one of Africa's largest independent churches.
causes: Bible-reading Baptist converts seeking African prophecy
consequences: Kimbanguist Church (EJCSK), member of WCC since 1969

events.title: Scopes Trial
events.summary: Teacher John Scopes was tried for teaching evolution contrary to Tennessee's Butler Act; William Jennings Bryan helped the prosecution and Clarence Darrow the defence. Scopes was convicted (later overturned on a technicality), but press coverage portrayed fundamentalists as backward, accelerating their withdrawal from mainline institutions.

events.title: Cristero War in Mexico
events.summary: Enforcement of the anticlerical articles of Mexico's 1917 constitution by President Calles led bishops to suspend public worship and Catholic peasants to rise up with the cry '¡Viva Cristo Rey!'. Around 90,000 died before a 1929 settlement; many martyrs, including the Jesuit Miguel Pro, were later beatified or canonised.

events.title: Aladura revival in Nigeria
events.summary: Joseph Ayo Babalola, a former road-roller driver, led a healing revival at Oke-Oye, Ilesa in 1930 that drew vast crowds. The Yoruba 'praying' (aladura) churches — Christ Apostolic Church, Cherubim and Seraphim, Church of the Lord (Aladura) — combined prayer, prophecy and healing with African forms.
causes: Dissatisfaction with mission churches' approach to healing

events.title: Barmen Declaration
events.summary: At a synod in Barmen, Lutheran, Reformed and United delegates of the Confessing Church adopted six theses, largely drafted by Karl Barth, rejecting the pro-Nazi 'German Christians': Jesus Christ is the one Word of God whom we must trust and obey. It did not explicitly mention the Jews, a silence later lamented.
causes: Nazi attempt to control the Protestant church
consequences: Model of confessional resistance (e.g., Kairos, Belhar)

events.title: Tambaram missionary conference
events.summary: The International Missionary Council met at Madras Christian College, Tambaram, with for the first time a majority of delegates from the 'younger churches' of Asia, Africa and Latin America. Hendrik Kraemer's book on the Christian message in a non-Christian world framed debate on religions.

events.title: Church of South India formed
events.summary: Anglicans, Methodists and the South India United Church (Presbyterian and Congregational) united on 27 September 1947, weeks after Indian independence, accepting episcopacy while recognising existing ministries. It was the first union of episcopal and non-episcopal churches.
causes: Indian church leaders' desire for unity beyond Western divisions
consequences: Model for Church of North India (1970) and other unions

events.title: World Council of Churches founded
events.summary: Some 147 churches met in Amsterdam to form the WCC, uniting the Faith and Order and Life and Work movements. Most Orthodox churches joined by 1961; the Catholic Church is not a member but cooperates. Many evangelicals and Pentecostals remained critical of its theology and social activism.

events.title: Dogma of the Assumption of Mary
events.summary: In Munificentissimus Deus (1 November 1950) Pius XII defined that Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory — the only universally recognised ex cathedra definition after 1870. Orthodox believe in her Dormition and bodily assumption but reject the papal definition; Protestants mostly reject the doctrine as unbiblical.

events.title: Three-Self Patriotic Movement formalised
events.summary: After the 1950 'Christian Manifesto' and expulsion of foreign missionaries, China's Protestants were organised under the state-sanctioned Three-Self (self-governing, self-supporting, self-propagating) Patriotic Movement. Christians refusing registration, such as Wang Mingdao and Watchman Nee's Little Flock, were imprisoned; unregistered 'house churches' grew.

events.title: Yoido Full Gospel Church founded
events.summary: David Yonggi Cho and Choi Ja-shil began a tent church in a Seoul slum in 1958 preaching healing, prosperity and the 'fourfold gospel'. Moving to Yeouido island in 1973 and organised through cell groups, it grew to some 800,000 members by the 2000s, the largest congregation in the world.

events.title: Charismatic renewal begins in historic churches
events.summary: Episcopal rector Dennis Bennett's announcement on Passion Sunday 1960 that he had spoken in tongues marked the public start of the charismatic movement in mainline churches. Catholic renewal followed at Duquesne University in 1967; by the 1980s charismatics were found in nearly every tradition.
causes: Pentecostal influence through Full Gospel Business Men

events.title: Second Vatican Council
events.summary: Called by John XXIII for aggiornamento (updating), some 2,500 bishops from every continent produced sixteen documents on liturgy, revelation, the church and the modern world. Vernacular liturgy, collegiality, religious freedom, ecumenism and a new stance toward Judaism and other religions reshaped global Catholicism.
events.longText: Vatican II was the first truly global council, with bishops from Africa, Asia and Latin America and observers from Orthodox and Protestant churches. Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963) called for 'full, conscious and active participation' and opened the way for vernacular Mass. Dei Verbum taught that Scripture and Tradition form one sacred deposit and encouraged biblical scholarship. Lumen Gentium described the church as the people of God and a sacrament of salvation, affirmed episcopal collegiality and the universal call to holiness, and said the church of Christ 'subsists in' the Catholic Church while elements of truth exist beyond it. Unitatis Redintegratio called other Christians 'separated brethren'; Nostra Aetate repudiated blaming Jews collectively for Christ's death; Dignitatis Humanae affirmed religious freedom; Gaudium et Spes engaged the modern world. Interpretation remains contested: progressives saw an unfinished revolution, traditionalists (notably Archbishop Lefebvre) a rupture, and Popes Benedict XVI and Francis spoke of a 'hermeneutic of reform' in continuity. Many Protestants welcomed the Bible-centred liturgy and ecumenical openness while noting that core doctrinal differences remained.

events.title: Cultural Revolution in China
events.summary: Mao's Cultural Revolution closed all churches, including Three-Self ones; Bibles were burned and clergy sent to labour camps. Christianity survived in secret home gatherings and, after 1979, emerged much larger, especially in rural house-church networks.

events.title: Medellín Conference of Latin American bishops
events.summary: The second general conference of CELAM applied Vatican II to a continent of poverty and dictatorship, denouncing 'institutionalised violence' and endorsing base ecclesial communities and a preferential concern for the poor. It gave momentum to liberation theology, formulated by Gustavo Gutiérrez in 1971.

events.title: Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization
events.summary: Convened by Billy Graham, 2,700 evangelicals from 150 countries adopted the Lausanne Covenant, chiefly drafted by John Stott. Latin American voices such as René Padilla and Samuel Escobar pressed for social responsibility alongside evangelism; Ralph Winter introduced 'unreached people groups'.

events.title: Assassination of Óscar Romero
events.summary: Archbishop Óscar Romero of San Salvador, who had become an outspoken defender of the poor against the military regime, was shot dead while celebrating Mass on 24 March 1980. He was canonised in 2018 and is honoured across denominations as a modern martyr.

events.title: Kairos Document in South Africa
events.summary: Black South African theologians in Soweto issued the Kairos Document, criticising 'state theology' that justified apartheid and 'church theology' that sought cheap reconciliation, and calling for prophetic theology. Alongside Desmond Tutu's leadership and the Belhar Confession, churches helped bring apartheid to an end.
consequences: Church role in transition; Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996)

events.title: Millennium of the Baptism of Rus' and Orthodox revival
events.summary: Gorbachev permitted public celebration of the millennium of Rus' baptism, signalling an end to Soviet persecution. After 1991 thousands of churches and monasteries reopened across Russia, Ukraine and Belarus, though Orthodoxy's close ties to the Russian state became contested.

events.title: Common Christological Declaration with the Assyrian Church of the East
events.summary: Pope John Paul II and Catholicos-Patriarch Mar Dinkha IV signed a declaration recognising that Catholics and the Assyrian Church of the East confess the same faith in Christ, true God and true man, despite different terms (Theotokos vs 'Mother of Christ our God and Saviour'). It ended a division dating to 431 at the level of Christology.
consequences: Agreed Guidelines on Eucharistic admission with the Chaldean Church (2001)

events.title: Toronto Blessing
events.summary: From January 1994 meetings at the Toronto Airport Vineyard church led by John and Carol Arnott featured 'holy laughter', falling, shaking and animal-like noises interpreted as a refreshing of the Holy Spirit. Hundreds of thousands visited; John Wimber's Vineyard disaffiliated the church in 1995, and critics questioned the phenomena.
consequences: Spread to Holy Trinity Brompton and globally

events.title: Brownsville Revival
events.summary: Beginning on Father's Day 1995 at Brownsville Assembly of God, evangelist Steve Hill's preaching on repentance launched nightly meetings over five years that drew an estimated 2.5 million visitors. Supporters reported conversions and restored lives; critics questioned manifestations and reported numbers.

events.title: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification
events.summary: On Reformation Day 1999 the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed a declaration stating a 'consensus in basic truths' on justification — by grace alone, through faith, not because of any merit — and that the 16th-century condemnations do not apply to the teaching it presents. Methodists (2006), Reformed (2017) and Anglicans (2016/17) later associated themselves.
consequences: Critiques from confessional Lutherans and some Catholics

events.title: Election of Pope Francis, first Latin American pope
events.summary: Jorge Mario Bergoglio, Jesuit archbishop of Buenos Aires, was elected pope on 13 March 2013, the first from the Americas and the global South. His emphasis on mercy, the poor, the environment (Laudato si', 2015) and synodality reflected the shift of Catholicism's centre of gravity southward.
causes: Growth of Catholicism in the global South
consequences: Debates between progressive and traditionalist Catholics

events.title: Christians expelled from Mosul and the Nineveh Plains
events.summary: In July–August 2014 the so-called Islamic State ordered Christians in Mosul to convert, pay jizya or leave, and then overran the Nineveh Plains, driving out some 120,000 Chaldean, Syriac and Assyrian Christians. It accelerated the collapse of Iraq's Christian population from over a million before 2003.
consequences: Near-extinction of ancient Christian communities in Iraq and Syria

events.title: Holy and Great Council of Crete
events.summary: After decades of preparation, ten autocephalous Orthodox churches met under Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew at Kolymbari. The churches of Russia, Antioch, Georgia and Bulgaria withdrew shortly before, exposing tensions over primacy within Orthodoxy.
consequences: Documents on mission, diaspora, marriage and relations with other Christians

events.title: Autocephaly of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine
events.summary: The Ecumenical Patriarchate granted a tomos of autocephaly to the newly united Orthodox Church of Ukraine in January 2019. The Moscow Patriarchate broke communion with Constantinople, deepening a schism within world Orthodoxy that worsened after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

events.title: Asbury Revival
events.summary: After a routine chapel service on 8 February 2023 at Asbury University, students remained to pray, sing and confess for about two weeks of continuous worship that drew an estimated 50,000 visitors. Leaders deliberately avoided celebrity preachers; observers debated whether it constituted 'revival' and how much social media amplified it.
consequences: Discussion of revival in a digital age
